analysis.one_liner: Lets the president negotiate trade deals Congress can only approve or reject without changing.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by a single vote, 215-214, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would revive "fast-track" trade authority (also called trade promotion authority), which lets the president negotiate trade agreements with other countries and then send them to Congress for a yes-or-no vote with no amendments allowed. It sets negotiating goals for the president, including lower tariffs abroad, stronger protection for patents and other intellectual property, and provisions on labor and the environment, and it authorizes agreements through mid-2005, extendable to 2007. Deals covering goods the president could not fully change by proclamation would still need a law passed by Congress, but Congress could not rewrite the deal itself.
analysis.who_benefits: Exporters, multinational firms, and intellectual-property-heavy industries gain the most. Fast-track authority makes trade deals credible and passable, and the bill's stated negotiating objectives include opening foreign markets, protecting patents and copyrights, and pressuring other countries to drop measures like drug price controls. Agribusiness gains from export-focused agriculture objectives. Consumers can benefit from lower prices on imported goods.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the president to negotiate agreements reducing tariffs and other trade barriers before June 1, 2005, extendable to June 1, 2007, with Congress voting up or down on an implementing bill that cannot be amended.

Sets negotiating objectives to reduce foreign trade barriers, protect intellectual property at U.S. standards, and eliminate foreign government measures such as price controls that limit market access for U.S. products.
Directs negotiators to seek rules that trading partners do not weaken domestic environmental and labor laws to attract trade, and requires environmental and employment reviews of future agreements.
Creates a Congressional Oversight Group of lawmakers who serve as advisers to U.S. trade negotiators and requires the president to submit an implementation and enforcement plan with each agreement.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in import-competing industries bear the risk of job losses from deals they could not amend, and the labor and environmental protections in the bill are largely aspirational: parties only 'strive' not to weaken their laws, and a country can claim it is 'effectively enforcing' them through reasonable discretion over enforcement. Congress also gives up its power to change trade deals, leaving members a single up-or-down vote on texts negotiated mostly in private.
analysis.who_pays_short: Import-competing workers and Congress's own authority

drawbacks.text: Under the bill's trade authorities procedures, Congress votes on an implementing bill without the ability to amend it, so members must accept or reject an entire negotiated package as-is.

The labor and environment provisions are weak: parties only 'strive' not to reduce domestic protections, and the bill states that no retaliation may be based on a country's 'reasonable exercise' of enforcement discretion, making the standards hard to enforce.

The bill directs negotiators to seek elimination of foreign price controls and reference pricing for U.S. products, a provision that chiefly benefits pharmaceutical and other firms selling into markets where governments negotiate lower prices.

The investment chapter directs negotiators to secure investor protections and dispute mechanisms for foreign investors in U.S. law, the framework that lets investors bring arbitration claims against governments over regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real upside: market openings for exporters, cheaper goods for consumers, and a seat for Congress in the negotiating room through the oversight group. But the structure of the bill tips heavily toward industries that trade internationally. The provisions that mattered most to workers and environmental advocates were non-binding 'strive to' language and consultation requirements, while the binding parts were the procedures guaranteeing tariff cuts and a no-amendment vote on each deal. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this is a bill about process power, and the process power flows to the president and to internationally competitive firms.

outcome.mechanism: It squeaked through the House 215-214 with almost no Democratic support, the Senate Finance Committee rewrote and reported it favorably, but the Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill by a single vote, 215-214, with 194 of 223 House Republicans voting yes and only 21 of 211 voting Democrats joining them.
Before the final vote, Democrats moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions; that motion failed 162-267, with 161 House Democrats in favor and no Republicans.
The bill's rules debate was closed to amendments, with only a motion to recommit allowed, limiting members to an up-or-down choice.
The Senate Finance Committee considered and marked up the bill, then reported it favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute in February 2002 and placed it on the Senate calendar.
The bill sat on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders and never received a Senate floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
Congress later enacted trade promotion authority that same year through a separate bill, so the policy itself ultimately became law despite this bill's death in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, opponents of fast-track authority won the delay, and import-competing industries and their workers were spared a Senate vote they likely could not stop. But the win was temporary: a version of trade promotion authority was enacted later in 2002 through another bill, so the exporters and multinational firms the authority serves ended up with what they wanted anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents won a delay, but TPA passed later that year

sides.party_line_note: House passage split sharply by party, 194-23 among Republicans and 21-189 among Democrats, for a one-vote margin of 215-214; the Senate never reached a floor vote.

industries.industry: Multinational exporters and internationally traded service firms
industries.note: Fast-track authority makes trade deals negotiable and passable, opening foreign markets for firms that sell abroad. Consumers share some benefit through lower prices, while import-competing workers absorb the adjustment costs.

industries.industry: Brand-name pharmaceutical and other intellectual-property-intensive firms
industries.note: The bill directs negotiators to extend U.S.-style IP protections abroad and to eliminate foreign price controls and reference pricing that limit U.S. product sales. That directly targets the government programs that hold drug prices down in other countries.
The bill sets detailed objectives for reducing foreign agricultural tariffs and subsidies and preserving U.S. export credit and market development programs, aiming to expand farm exports.

industries.industry: Import-competing manufacturers and textile and apparel producers
industries.note: The bill contains staging limits on tariff cuts and special consultation requirements for textiles and import-sensitive agricultural products, but the overall thrust is further tariff reduction, and negotiated deals could not be amended to add protections.

The bill's core labor standards language is aspirational and its enforcement objective expressly bars retaliation based on a country's reasonable enforcement discretion, leaving unions with fewer tools to contest deals negotiated without amendments.
